Ordered outcomes

Source: vignettes/ordered-outcomes.Rmd
ordered-outcomes.Rmd

Many spatial panel outcomes are ordered categories: credit ratings, survey scales, damage levels, land-use intensity. psoprobit() fits the spatial ordered probit model. It uses the same arguments as psprobit() (see vignette("getting-started")), so this vignette concentrates on what is specific to ordered outcomes.

library(panelspatialprobit)

The model

The latent model is the same as in the binary case,

zt=ρWzt+Xtβ+WXtθ+α+εt,εt∼N(0,IN),z_t = \rho W z_t + X_t\beta + W X_t\theta + \alpha + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0, I_N),

and the observed category is yit=jy_{it} = j when κj−1<zit≤κj\kappa_{j-1} < z_{it} \le \kappa_j, for j=1,…,Jj = 1, \dots, J, with κ0=−∞\kappa_0 = -\infty and κJ=+∞\kappa_J = +\infty.

Identification. The model includes an intercept, so the first cut-point is fixed at κ1=0\kappa_1 = 0, and the free cut-points are 0<κ2<…<κJ−10 < \kappa_2 < \dots < \kappa_{J-1} (named cut[2|3], cut[3|4], …). This is the parameterisation of MCMCpack::MCMCoprobit. Packages such as MASS::polr and ordinal::clm drop the intercept and estimate all J−1J - 1 thresholds instead; summary() reports the thresholds in that parameterisation too, ζj=κj−β0\zeta_j = \kappa_j - \beta_0.

The response can be an ordered factor, a factor (its level order is used) or integer codes. Every category must occur in the data.

Example

We simulate J=4J = 4 categories on a 10 × 10 grid observed over 5 periods:

W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(10, 10), style = "W")
d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 5, beta = c(0.2, 1, -0.8), rho = 0.5, sigma_alpha = 0.6,
                  cutpoints = c(0.8, 1.6), seed = 7)
d$y <- factor(d$y, labels = c("none", "low", "medium", "high"), ordered = TRUE)
table(d$y)
#> 
#>   none    low medium   high 
#>    216     80     68    136
fit <- psoprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                 control = psp_control(iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2,
                                       seed = 1, progress = FALSE))
summary(fit)
#> Bayesian panel spatial ordered probit (model = sar, effects = random) 
#> Call: psoprobit(formula = y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"),

The truth is β=(0.2,1,−0.8)\beta = (0.2, 1, -0.8), ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5, σα=0.6\sigma_\alpha = 0.6 and cut-points (0,0.8,1.6)(0, 0.8, 1.6).

Impacts per category

A regressor moves probability mass between categories: if it raises the latent outcome, the top categories become more likely and the bottom ones less likely. Impacts are therefore reported per category and, for each regressor and effect type, sum to zero over the categories.

imp <- fit$impacts
s <- summary(imp)
s[s$variable == "x1" & s$effect == "total", c("category", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")]
#>    category          mean        q2.5       q97.5
#> 17     none -0.3970782465 -0.46653413 -0.33591238
#> 19      low  0.0004226489 -0.02845663  0.02705857
#> 21   medium  0.0565979051  0.03058806  0.08141688
#> 23     high  0.3400576925  0.27881770  0.41981368
sum(s$mean[s$variable == "x1" & s$effect == "total"])
#> [1] -3.122502e-17

The options of psp_impacts() (type = "unit", by_period = TRUE, scale = "lesage_pace") work as for binary models.

Predicted probabilities

predict(type = "prob") returns an NT×JNT \times J matrix of posterior mean category probabilities, in the row order of the data; type = "class" returns the most probable category.

head(round(predict(fit), 3))
#>       none   low medium  high
#> [1,] 0.015 0.039  0.092 0.854
#> [2,] 0.426 0.227  0.179 0.168
#> [3,] 0.442 0.230  0.175 0.153
#> [4,] 0.752 0.146  0.070 0.033
#> [5,] 0.324 0.229  0.209 0.239
#> [6,] 0.097 0.141  0.208 0.555
psp_classification(fit)$confusion
#>         predicted
#> observed none low medium high
#>   none    194   0      0   22
#>   low      56   0      0   24
#>   medium   31   0      0   37
#>   high     23   0      0  113

The cut-point sampler

Updating the cut-points one at a time given the latent values (Albert and Chib 1993) mixes slowly when there are many observations, because each cut-point is squeezed between the latent values of the neighbouring categories. The default sampler (cutpoint_sampler = "transform") adds a joint Metropolis–Hastings move that shifts a cut-point and rescales the latent values of the two adjacent categories with it (Liu and Sabatti 2000), so the cut-point can move far in one step. Its step size is tuned during warm-up; the acceptance rates after warm-up are stored in the fit:

fit$cut_accept
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.2343333 0.3120000
#> [2,] 0.3496667 0.4353333

cutpoint_sampler = "albert_chib" uses the Gibbs step alone. Both samplers target the same posterior and pass simulation-based calibration; the transformation move gives a higher effective sample size per second for the cut-points, by up to two orders of magnitude for interior cut-points (see vignette("validation")).

Priors on the cut-points

The default prior is N(0,102)N(0, 10^2) on each free cut-point, restricted to the ordering constraint. psp_priors(cutpoints = prior_flat()) uses a flat prior, as MCMCpack::MCMCoprobit does.

References

Albert, J. H. and Chib, S. (1993). Bayesian analysis of binary and polychotomous response data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 88, 669–679.

LeSage, J. P., Pace, R. K., Lam, N., Campanella, R. and Liu, X. (2011). New Orleans business recovery in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A 174, 1007–1027.

Liu, J. S. and Sabatti, C. (2000). Generalised Gibbs sampler and multigrid Monte Carlo for Bayesian computation. Biometrika 87, 353–369.
